## Debt Buyer Rights in Maryland [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses
Source: https://debtbuyerrights.org/states/maryland.html

← debtbuyerrights.org home

Debt Buyer Rights in Maryland [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Maryland residents.

Debt Buyers in Maryland

Maryland has one of the stronger debt-buyer regulatory frameworks in the US. Junk debt buyers filing suit on purchased accounts face documented pleading and proof requirements that are often insurmountable when the original creditor's records are lost.

A "debt buyer" (also called a junk debt buyer, JDB, or debt purchaser) is a company that buys charged-off consumer debt from original creditors for pennies on the dollar - typically 3-5 cents per dollar face value - and attempts to collect the full balance. Common Maryland debt buyers include Midland Funding, LVNV Funding, Portfolio Recovery Associates, Cavalry SPV, and Jefferson Capital Systems.

Maryland Licensing Regime

Licensing: Debt collector license under Maryland Collection Agency Licensing Act (Md. Code Bus. Reg. Title 7).

Chain-of-title standard: MD case law requires substantial chain of title; Finch v. LVNV decisions require proof.

Applicable consumer statute: Maryland Consumer Debt Collection Act (Md. Code Comm. Law 14-201).

Unlicensed collection activity in Maryland is itself an actionable violation in most cases - both as an independent state claim and as an FDCPA violation (because federal law prohibits collecting "by any means" that is illegal under state law).

FDCPA and Chain-of-Title Proof

Federal FDCPA (15 U.S.C. Section 1692g) and state law in Maryland generally require a debt buyer to produce:

The original cardholder agreement - proving the account existed and terms were agreed to.

Billing statements showing activity, charges, and last payment date.

Charge-off statement - the balance at the moment the original creditor wrote off the debt.

Assignment documentation - each transfer from original creditor through any intermediaries to the current plaintiff.

Bill of sale and purchase agreement showing the specific account is included in the sold portfolio.

Affidavits from each transferring entity's records custodian.

In contested Maryland cases, one or more of these links is frequently missing. Missing links = no enforceable debt. See proof-of-debt checklist.

Maryland Defenses to Junk Debt Suits

If a debt buyer has filed suit against you in Maryland, available defenses include:

Failure to state a claim. Complaint lacks specific allegations about the original creditor, assignment chain, or account details.

Standing. JDB cannot prove it owns your specific account; only owns a portfolio generally.

Statute of limitations. If the last legitimate activity was more than the state SOL years ago, the debt is time-barred. See Maryland credit card SOL.

Account stated rejection. Challenge whether the final balance was ever agreed to.

Usury/unlawful fees. Fees added post-charge-off may be challengeable.

Unlicensed collection. If the JDB lacks required Maryland licensing, collection itself may be void.

FDCPA counterclaim. Filing a time-barred suit or misrepresenting the debt can trigger $1,000 statutory damages plus attorney fees.

See SOL defense mechanics and when to fight.

Maryland Debt Buyer Settlement Economics

Maryland debt buyers paid 3-5 cents per dollar for your account. A settlement at 20-40% of face value is therefore extremely profitable for them - and still provides real relief to you:

Opening offer: JDBs typically accept 20-40% of claimed balance.

Pre-suit: Settlement range 30-50%; avoid the suit entirely.

Post-suit, pre-judgment: 40-60%; courthouse settlement common.

Post-judgment: 50-70%; execution risk drives urgency.

Always insist on: (1) written settlement agreement identifying the specific debt, (2) dismissal with prejudice if suit was filed, (3) confirmation the account will be reported as "Paid for Less than Full Balance" or "Paid/Settled" (not "Paid in Full" unless you negotiated that), and (4) no 1099-C unless the forgiveness exceeds $600 and you accept the tax hit.

See settlement strategy playbook.

Maryland Federal Bankruptcy Data

When defending a debt buyer is not enough - because multiple JDB suits are pending, or the original creditor assignments are stronger than expected - bankruptcy extinguishes the underlying debt. These FJC numbers show how Maryland debtors actually resolve junk debt.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 559 consumer bankruptcy cases from Maryland's federal bankruptcy courts.

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

When Bankruptcy Defeats Maryland Debt Buyers

Bankruptcy has several advantages over defending each JDB suit individually:

Automatic stay. All JDB lawsuits freeze instantly on filing under 11 U.S.C. Section 362.

Discharge. Most JDB-held consumer debt is unsecured and fully discharged under Section 727 (Ch 7) or 1328 (Ch 13).

Schedule F reaches all creditors. You do not need to track each JDB suit separately.

Proof of claim reversal. In bankruptcy, the JDB must produce the same chain-of-title documentation or the claim can be disallowed under 11 U.S.C. Section 502. You can object and win even without full litigation.

No post-discharge contact. Discharged debt cannot be collected; JDBs attempting to collect violate 11 U.S.C. Section 524 and face contempt sanctions.

See proof of debt in bankruptcy and Maryland credit card bankruptcy.

Many JDB operations use layered corporate structures: LVNV Funding operates with Resurgent Capital; Midland Funding operates with Midland Credit Management; Portfolio Recovery uses multiple affiliates. This layering can complicate chain-of-title proofs and creates enforcement targets under Maryland consumer statutes.

When responding to a Maryland JDB suit, research the plaintiff's corporate parent and related entities. Inconsistent naming between the complaint, underlying agreement, and affidavit is grounds for dismissal in many Maryland courts. See shell company deep-dive.

Debt Buyer Rights in Minnesota [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Minnesota residents.

Debt Buyers in Minnesota

Minnesota has one of the stronger debt-buyer regulatory frameworks in the US. Junk debt buyers filing suit on purchased accounts face documented pleading and proof requirements that are often insurmountable when the original creditor's records are lost.

Minnesota Licensing Regime

Licensing: Debt Buyer Registration (Minn. Stat. 332.37) + specific debt buyer pleading requirements (Minn. Stat. 548.101).

Chain-of-title standard: MN requires debt buyer plaintiffs to attach chain-of-title documentation to complaint.

Applicable consumer statute: Minnesota Debt Buyer Act + Minnesota Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

Unlicensed collection activity in Minnesota is itself an actionable violation in most cases - both as an independent state claim and as an FDCPA violation (because federal law prohibits collecting "by any means" that is illegal under state law).

## Debt Buyer Rights in Mississippi [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses
Source: https://debtbuyerrights.org/states/mississippi.html

← debtbuyerrights.org home

Debt Buyer Rights in Mississippi [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Mississippi residents.

Debt Buyers in Mississippi

Mississippi regulates debt buyers primarily through general collection-agency rules rather than a dedicated junk-debt-buyer statute. Federal FDCPA and evidence-rule defenses still apply powerfully.

A "debt buyer" (also called a junk debt buyer, JDB, or debt purchaser) is a company that buys charged-off consumer debt from original creditors for pennies on the dollar - typically 3-5 cents per dollar face value - and attempts to collect the full balance. Common Mississippi debt buyers include Midland Funding, LVNV Funding, Portfolio Recovery Associates, Cavalry SPV, and Jefferson Capital Systems.

Mississippi Licensing Regime

Licensing: General collection rules; no dedicated debt-buyer statute.

Chain-of-title standard: Evidence rules control.

Applicable consumer statute: Mississippi Consumer Protection Act (Miss. Code 75-24).

Unlicensed collection activity in Mississippi is itself an actionable violation in most cases - both as an independent state claim and as an FDCPA violation (because federal law prohibits collecting "by any means" that is illegal under state law).

FDCPA and Chain-of-Title Proof

Federal FDCPA (15 U.S.C. Section 1692g) and state law in Mississippi generally require a debt buyer to produce:

The original cardholder agreement - proving the account existed and terms were agreed to.

Billing statements showing activity, charges, and last payment date.

Charge-off statement - the balance at the moment the original creditor wrote off the debt.

Assignment documentation - each transfer from original creditor through any intermediaries to the current plaintiff.

Bill of sale and purchase agreement showing the specific account is included in the sold portfolio.

Affidavits from each transferring entity's records custodian.

In contested Mississippi cases, one or more of these links is frequently missing. Missing links = no enforceable debt. See proof-of-debt checklist.

Mississippi Defenses to Junk Debt Suits

If a debt buyer has filed suit against you in Mississippi, available defenses include:

Failure to state a claim. Complaint lacks specific allegations about the original creditor, assignment chain, or account details.

Standing. JDB cannot prove it owns your specific account; only owns a portfolio generally.

Statute of limitations. If the last legitimate activity was more than the state SOL years ago, the debt is time-barred. See Mississippi credit card SOL.

Account stated rejection. Challenge whether the final balance was ever agreed to.

Usury/unlawful fees. Fees added post-charge-off may be challengeable.

Unlicensed collection. If the JDB lacks required Mississippi licensing, collection itself may be void.

FDCPA counterclaim. Filing a time-barred suit or misrepresenting the debt can trigger $1,000 statutory damages plus attorney fees.

See SOL defense mechanics and when to fight.

Mississippi Debt Buyer Settlement Economics

Mississippi debt buyers paid 3-5 cents per dollar for your account. A settlement at 20-40% of face value is therefore extremely profitable for them - and still provides real relief to you:

Opening offer: JDBs typically accept 20-40% of claimed balance.

Pre-suit: Settlement range 30-50%; avoid the suit entirely.

Post-suit, pre-judgment: 40-60%; courthouse settlement common.

Post-judgment: 50-70%; execution risk drives urgency.

Always insist on: (1) written settlement agreement identifying the specific debt, (2) dismissal with prejudice if suit was filed, (3) confirmation the account will be reported as "Paid for Less than Full Balance" or "Paid/Settled" (not "Paid in Full" unless you negotiated that), and (4) no 1099-C unless the forgiveness exceeds $600 and you accept the tax hit.

See settlement strategy playbook.

When Bankruptcy Defeats Mississippi Debt Buyers

Bankruptcy has several advantages over defending each JDB suit individually:

Automatic stay. All JDB lawsuits freeze instantly on filing under 11 U.S.C. Section 362.

Discharge. Most JDB-held consumer debt is unsecured and fully discharged under Section 727 (Ch 7) or 1328 (Ch 13).

Schedule F reaches all creditors. You do not need to track each JDB suit separately.

Proof of claim reversal. In bankruptcy, the JDB must produce the same chain-of-title documentation or the claim can be disallowed under 11 U.S.C. Section 502. You can object and win even without full litigation.

No post-discharge contact. Discharged debt cannot be collected; JDBs attempting to collect violate 11 U.S.C. Section 524 and face contempt sanctions.

See proof of debt in bankruptcy and Mississippi credit card bankruptcy.

Shell Companies and Affiliate Networks

Many JDB operations use layered corporate structures: LVNV Funding operates with Resurgent Capital; Midland Funding operates with Midland Credit Management; Portfolio Recovery uses multiple affiliates. This layering can complicate chain-of-title proofs and creates enforcement targets under Mississippi consumer statutes.

When responding to a Mississippi JDB suit, research the plaintiff's corporate parent and related entities. Inconsistent naming between the complaint, underlying agreement, and affidavit is grounds for dismissal in many Mississippi courts. See shell company deep-dive.

Related Mississippi Resources

Settlement strategies

## Debt Buyer Rights in Missouri [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses
Source: https://debtbuyerrights.org/states/missouri.html

← debtbuyerrights.org home

Debt Buyer Rights in Missouri [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Missouri residents.

Debt Buyers in Missouri

Missouri requires debt buyers to hold a collection-agency license and follow state collection statutes. Unlicensed operators and those with broken chains of title can be defeated using FDCPA and state UDAP claims.

A "debt buyer" (also called a junk debt buyer, JDB, or debt purchaser) is a company that buys charged-off consumer debt from original creditors for pennies on the dollar - typically 3-5 cents per dollar face value - and attempts to collect the full balance. Common Missouri debt buyers include Midland Funding, LVNV Funding, Portfolio Recovery Associates, Cavalry SPV, and Jefferson Capital Systems.

Missouri Licensing Regime

Licensing: Collection agency registration (RSMo 425).

Chain-of-title standard: Evidence rules control.

Applicable consumer statute: Missouri Merchandising Practices Act (RSMo 407.020).

Unlicensed collection activity in Missouri is itself an actionable violation in most cases - both as an independent state claim and as an FDCPA violation (because federal law prohibits collecting "by any means" that is illegal under state law).

FDCPA and Chain-of-Title Proof

Federal FDCPA (15 U.S.C. Section 1692g) and state law in Missouri generally require a debt buyer to produce:

The original cardholder agreement - proving the account existed and terms were agreed to.

Billing statements showing activity, charges, and last payment date.

Charge-off statement - the balance at the moment the original creditor wrote off the debt.

Assignment documentation - each transfer from original creditor through any intermediaries to the current plaintiff.

Bill of sale and purchase agreement showing the specific account is included in the sold portfolio.

Affidavits from each transferring entity's records custodian.

In contested Missouri cases, one or more of these links is frequently missing. Missing links = no enforceable debt. See proof-of-debt checklist.

Missouri Defenses to Junk Debt Suits

If a debt buyer has filed suit against you in Missouri, available defenses include:

Failure to state a claim. Complaint lacks specific allegations about the original creditor, assignment chain, or account details.

Standing. JDB cannot prove it owns your specific account; only owns a portfolio generally.

Statute of limitations. If the last legitimate activity was more than the state SOL years ago, the debt is time-barred. See Missouri credit card SOL.

Account stated rejection. Challenge whether the final balance was ever agreed to.

Usury/unlawful fees. Fees added post-charge-off may be challengeable.

Unlicensed collection. If the JDB lacks required Missouri licensing, collection itself may be void.

FDCPA counterclaim. Filing a time-barred suit or misrepresenting the debt can trigger $1,000 statutory damages plus attorney fees.

See SOL defense mechanics and when to fight.

Missouri Debt Buyer Settlement Economics

Missouri debt buyers paid 3-5 cents per dollar for your account. A settlement at 20-40% of face value is therefore extremely profitable for them - and still provides real relief to you:

Opening offer: JDBs typically accept 20-40% of claimed balance.

Pre-suit: Settlement range 30-50%; avoid the suit entirely.

Post-suit, pre-judgment: 40-60%; courthouse settlement common.

Post-judgment: 50-70%; execution risk drives urgency.

Always insist on: (1) written settlement agreement identifying the specific debt, (2) dismissal with prejudice if suit was filed, (3) confirmation the account will be reported as "Paid for Less than Full Balance" or "Paid/Settled" (not "Paid in Full" unless you negotiated that), and (4) no 1099-C unless the forgiveness exceeds $600 and you accept the tax hit.

See settlement strategy playbook.

Missouri Federal Bankruptcy Data

When defending a debt buyer is not enough - because multiple JDB suits are pending, or the original creditor assignments are stronger than expected - bankruptcy extinguishes the underlying debt. These FJC numbers show how Missouri debtors actually resolve junk debt.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 45,771 consumer bankruptcy cases from Missouri's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 722,13299.0%0.8%

Chapter 1323,63955.1%44.7%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

When Bankruptcy Defeats Missouri Debt Buyers

Bankruptcy has several advantages over defending each JDB suit individually:

Automatic stay. All JDB lawsuits freeze instantly on filing under 11 U.S.C. Section 362.

Discharge. Most JDB-held consumer debt is unsecured and fully discharged under Section 727 (Ch 7) or 1328 (Ch 13).

Schedule F reaches all creditors. You do not need to track each JDB suit separately.

Proof of claim reversal. In bankruptcy, the JDB must produce the same chain-of-title documentation or the claim can be disallowed under 11 U.S.C. Section 502. You can object and win even without full litigation.

No post-discharge contact. Discharged debt cannot be collected; JDBs attempting to collect violate 11 U.S.C. Section 524 and face contempt sanctions.

See proof of debt in bankruptcy and Missouri credit card bankruptcy.

Shell Companies and Affiliate Networks

Many JDB operations use layered corporate structures: LVNV Funding operates with Resurgent Capital; Midland Funding operates with Midland Credit Management; Portfolio Recovery uses multiple affiliates. This layering can complicate chain-of-title proofs and creates enforcement targets under Missouri consumer statutes.

When responding to a Missouri JDB suit, research the plaintiff's corporate parent and related entities. Inconsistent naming between the complaint, underlying agreement, and affidavit is grounds for dismissal in many Missouri courts. See shell company deep-dive.

## Debt Buyer Rights in New Hampshire [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses
Source: https://debtbuyerrights.org/states/new-hampshire.html

← debtbuyerrights.org home

Debt Buyer Rights in New Hampshire [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Hampshire residents.

Debt Buyers in New Hampshire

New Hampshire requires debt buyers to hold a collection-agency license and follow state collection statutes. Unlicensed operators and those with broken chains of title can be defeated using FDCPA and state UDAP claims.

A "debt buyer" (also called a junk debt buyer, JDB, or debt purchaser) is a company that buys charged-off consumer debt from original creditors for pennies on the dollar - typically 3-5 cents per dollar face value - and attempts to collect the full balance. Common New Hampshire debt buyers include Midland Funding, LVNV Funding, Portfolio Recovery Associates, Cavalry SPV, and Jefferson Capital Systems.

New Hampshire Licensing Regime

Licensing: Collection agency license (RSA 358-C).

Chain-of-title standard: Evidence rules control.

Applicable consumer statute: New Hampshire Consumer Protection Act (RSA 358-A).

Unlicensed collection activity in New Hampshire is itself an actionable violation in most cases - both as an independent state claim and as an FDCPA violation (because federal law prohibits collecting "by any means" that is illegal under state law).

FDCPA and Chain-of-Title Proof

Federal FDCPA (15 U.S.C. Section 1692g) and state law in New Hampshire generally require a debt buyer to produce:

The original cardholder agreement - proving the account existed and terms were agreed to.

Billing statements showing activity, charges, and last payment date.

Charge-off statement - the balance at the moment the original creditor wrote off the debt.

Assignment documentation - each transfer from original creditor through any intermediaries to the current plaintiff.

Bill of sale and purchase agreement showing the specific account is included in the sold portfolio.

Affidavits from each transferring entity's records custodian.

In contested New Hampshire cases, one or more of these links is frequently missing. Missing links = no enforceable debt. See proof-of-debt checklist.

New Hampshire Defenses to Junk Debt Suits

If a debt buyer has filed suit against you in New Hampshire, available defenses include:

Failure to state a claim. Complaint lacks specific allegations about the original creditor, assignment chain, or account details.

Standing. JDB cannot prove it owns your specific account; only owns a portfolio generally.

Statute of limitations. If the last legitimate activity was more than the state SOL years ago, the debt is time-barred. See New Hampshire credit card SOL.

Account stated rejection. Challenge whether the final balance was ever agreed to.

Usury/unlawful fees. Fees added post-charge-off may be challengeable.

Unlicensed collection. If the JDB lacks required New Hampshire licensing, collection itself may be void.

FDCPA counterclaim. Filing a time-barred suit or misrepresenting the debt can trigger $1,000 statutory damages plus attorney fees.

See SOL defense mechanics and when to fight.

New Hampshire Debt Buyer Settlement Economics

New Hampshire debt buyers paid 3-5 cents per dollar for your account. A settlement at 20-40% of face value is therefore extremely profitable for them - and still provides real relief to you:

Opening offer: JDBs typically accept 20-40% of claimed balance.

Pre-suit: Settlement range 30-50%; avoid the suit entirely.

Post-suit, pre-judgment: 40-60%; courthouse settlement common.

Post-judgment: 50-70%; execution risk drives urgency.

Always insist on: (1) written settlement agreement identifying the specific debt, (2) dismissal with prejudice if suit was filed, (3) confirmation the account will be reported as "Paid for Less than Full Balance" or "Paid/Settled" (not "Paid in Full" unless you negotiated that), and (4) no 1099-C unless the forgiveness exceeds $600 and you accept the tax hit.

See settlement strategy playbook.

When Bankruptcy Defeats New Hampshire Debt Buyers

Bankruptcy has several advantages over defending each JDB suit individually:

Automatic stay. All JDB lawsuits freeze instantly on filing under 11 U.S.C. Section 362.

Discharge. Most JDB-held consumer debt is unsecured and fully discharged under Section 727 (Ch 7) or 1328 (Ch 13).

Schedule F reaches all creditors. You do not need to track each JDB suit separately.

Proof of claim reversal. In bankruptcy, the JDB must produce the same chain-of-title documentation or the claim can be disallowed under 11 U.S.C. Section 502. You can object and win even without full litigation.

No post-discharge contact. Discharged debt cannot be collected; JDBs attempting to collect violate 11 U.S.C. Section 524 and face contempt sanctions.

See proof of debt in bankruptcy and New Hampshire credit card bankruptcy.

Shell Companies and Affiliate Networks

Many JDB operations use layered corporate structures: LVNV Funding operates with Resurgent Capital; Midland Funding operates with Midland Credit Management; Portfolio Recovery uses multiple affiliates. This layering can complicate chain-of-title proofs and creates enforcement targets under New Hampshire consumer statutes.

When responding to a New Hampshire JDB suit, research the plaintiff's corporate parent and related entities. Inconsistent naming between the complaint, underlying agreement, and affidavit is grounds for dismissal in many New Hampshire courts. See shell company deep-dive.

Settlement strategies

## Debt Buyer Rights in New Jersey [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses
Source: https://debtbuyerrights.org/states/new-jersey.html

← debtbuyerrights.org home

Debt Buyer Rights in New Jersey [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Jersey residents.

Debt Buyers in New Jersey

New Jersey has one of the stronger debt-buyer regulatory frameworks in the US. Junk debt buyers filing suit on purchased accounts face documented pleading and proof requirements that are often insurmountable when the original creditor's records are lost.

A "debt buyer" (also called a junk debt buyer, JDB, or debt purchaser) is a company that buys charged-off consumer debt from original creditors for pennies on the dollar - typically 3-5 cents per dollar face value - and attempts to collect the full balance. Common New Jersey debt buyers include Midland Funding, LVNV Funding, Portfolio Recovery Associates, Cavalry SPV, and Jefferson Capital Systems.

New Jersey Licensing Regime

Licensing: Consumer Finance Licensing Act (N.J.S.A. 17:11C).

Chain-of-title standard: NJ case law (LVNV v. Osborne line) requires substantial chain-of-title documentation.

Applicable consumer statute: New Jersey Consumer Fraud Act (N.J.S.A. 56:8-1).

Unlicensed collection activity in New Jersey is itself an actionable violation in most cases - both as an independent state claim and as an FDCPA violation (because federal law prohibits collecting "by any means" that is illegal under state law).

FDCPA and Chain-of-Title Proof

Federal FDCPA (15 U.S.C. Section 1692g) and state law in New Jersey generally require a debt buyer to produce:

The original cardholder agreement - proving the account existed and terms were agreed to.

Billing statements showing activity, charges, and last payment date.

Charge-off statement - the balance at the moment the original creditor wrote off the debt.

Assignment documentation - each transfer from original creditor through any intermediaries to the current plaintiff.

Bill of sale and purchase agreement showing the specific account is included in the sold portfolio.

Affidavits from each transferring entity's records custodian.

In contested New Jersey cases, one or more of these links is frequently missing. Missing links = no enforceable debt. See proof-of-debt checklist.

New Jersey Defenses to Junk Debt Suits

If a debt buyer has filed suit against you in New Jersey, available defenses include:

Failure to state a claim. Complaint lacks specific allegations about the original creditor, assignment chain, or account details.

Standing. JDB cannot prove it owns your specific account; only owns a portfolio generally.

Statute of limitations. If the last legitimate activity was more than the state SOL years ago, the debt is time-barred. See New Jersey credit card SOL.

Account stated rejection. Challenge whether the final balance was ever agreed to.

Usury/unlawful fees. Fees added post-charge-off may be challengeable.

Unlicensed collection. If the JDB lacks required New Jersey licensing, collection itself may be void.

FDCPA counterclaim. Filing a time-barred suit or misrepresenting the debt can trigger $1,000 statutory damages plus attorney fees.

See SOL defense mechanics and when to fight.

New Jersey Debt Buyer Settlement Economics

New Jersey debt buyers paid 3-5 cents per dollar for your account. A settlement at 20-40% of face value is therefore extremely profitable for them - and still provides real relief to you:

Opening offer: JDBs typically accept 20-40% of claimed balance.

Pre-suit: Settlement range 30-50%; avoid the suit entirely.

Post-suit, pre-judgment: 40-60%; courthouse settlement common.

Post-judgment: 50-70%; execution risk drives urgency.

Always insist on: (1) written settlement agreement identifying the specific debt, (2) dismissal with prejudice if suit was filed, (3) confirmation the account will be reported as "Paid for Less than Full Balance" or "Paid/Settled" (not "Paid in Full" unless you negotiated that), and (4) no 1099-C unless the forgiveness exceeds $600 and you accept the tax hit.

See settlement strategy playbook.

New Jersey Federal Bankruptcy Data

When defending a debt buyer is not enough - because multiple JDB suits are pending, or the original creditor assignments are stronger than expected - bankruptcy extinguishes the underlying debt. These FJC numbers show how New Jersey debtors actually resolve junk debt.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,580 consumer bankruptcy cases from New Jersey's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 752697.3%2.7%

Chapter 131,05431.0%68.8%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

When Bankruptcy Defeats New Jersey Debt Buyers

Bankruptcy has several advantages over defending each JDB suit individually:

Automatic stay. All JDB lawsuits freeze instantly on filing under 11 U.S.C. Section 362.

Discharge. Most JDB-held consumer debt is unsecured and fully discharged under Section 727 (Ch 7) or 1328 (Ch 13).

Schedule F reaches all creditors. You do not need to track each JDB suit separately.

Proof of claim reversal. In bankruptcy, the JDB must produce the same chain-of-title documentation or the claim can be disallowed under 11 U.S.C. Section 502. You can object and win even without full litigation.

No post-discharge contact. Discharged debt cannot be collected; JDBs attempting to collect violate 11 U.S.C. Section 524 and face contempt sanctions.

See proof of debt in bankruptcy and New Jersey credit card bankruptcy.

Shell Companies and Affiliate Networks

Many JDB operations use layered corporate structures: LVNV Funding operates with Resurgent Capital; Midland Funding operates with Midland Credit Management; Portfolio Recovery uses multiple affiliates. This layering can complicate chain-of-title proofs and creates enforcement targets under New Jersey consumer statutes.

When responding to a New Jersey JDB suit, research the plaintiff's corporate parent and related entities. Inconsistent naming between the complaint, underlying agreement, and affidavit is grounds for dismissal in many New Jersey courts. See shell company deep-dive.

Debt Buyer Rights in New York [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New York residents.

Many JDB operations use layered corporate structures: LVNV Funding operates with Resurgent Capital; Midland Funding operates with Midland Credit Management; Portfolio Recovery uses multiple affiliates. This layering can complicate chain-of-title proofs and creates enforcement targets under North Carolina consumer statutes.

When responding to a North Carolina JDB suit, research the plaintiff's corporate parent and related entities. Inconsistent naming between the complaint, underlying agreement, and affidavit is grounds for dismissal in many North Carolina courts. See shell company deep-dive.

## Debt Buyer Rights in North Dakota [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses
Source: https://debtbuyerrights.org/states/north-dakota.html

← debtbuyerrights.org home

Debt Buyer Rights in North Dakota [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for North Dakota residents.

Debt Buyers in North Dakota

North Dakota requires debt buyers to hold a collection-agency license and follow state collection statutes. Unlicensed operators and those with broken chains of title can be defeated using FDCPA and state UDAP claims.

A "debt buyer" (also called a junk debt buyer, JDB, or debt purchaser) is a company that buys charged-off consumer debt from original creditors for pennies on the dollar - typically 3-5 cents per dollar face value - and attempts to collect the full balance. Common North Dakota debt buyers include Midland Funding, LVNV Funding, Portfolio Recovery Associates, Cavalry SPV, and Jefferson Capital Systems.

North Dakota Licensing Regime

Licensing: Collection agency license (NDCC 13-05).

Chain-of-title standard: Evidence rules control.

Applicable consumer statute: North Dakota Consumer Protection Act (NDCC 51-15).

Unlicensed collection activity in North Dakota is itself an actionable violation in most cases - both as an independent state claim and as an FDCPA violation (because federal law prohibits collecting "by any means" that is illegal under state law).

FDCPA and Chain-of-Title Proof

Federal FDCPA (15 U.S.C. Section 1692g) and state law in North Dakota generally require a debt buyer to produce:

The original cardholder agreement - proving the account existed and terms were agreed to.

Billing statements showing activity, charges, and last payment date.

Charge-off statement - the balance at the moment the original creditor wrote off the debt.

Assignment documentation - each transfer from original creditor through any intermediaries to the current plaintiff.

Bill of sale and purchase agreement showing the specific account is included in the sold portfolio.

Affidavits from each transferring entity's records custodian.

In contested North Dakota cases, one or more of these links is frequently missing. Missing links = no enforceable debt. See proof-of-debt checklist.

North Dakota Defenses to Junk Debt Suits

If a debt buyer has filed suit against you in North Dakota, available defenses include:

Failure to state a claim. Complaint lacks specific allegations about the original creditor, assignment chain, or account details.

Standing. JDB cannot prove it owns your specific account; only owns a portfolio generally.

Statute of limitations. If the last legitimate activity was more than the state SOL years ago, the debt is time-barred. See North Dakota credit card SOL.

Account stated rejection. Challenge whether the final balance was ever agreed to.

Usury/unlawful fees. Fees added post-charge-off may be challengeable.

Unlicensed collection. If the JDB lacks required North Dakota licensing, collection itself may be void.

FDCPA counterclaim. Filing a time-barred suit or misrepresenting the debt can trigger $1,000 statutory damages plus attorney fees.

See SOL defense mechanics and when to fight.

North Dakota Debt Buyer Settlement Economics

North Dakota debt buyers paid 3-5 cents per dollar for your account. A settlement at 20-40% of face value is therefore extremely profitable for them - and still provides real relief to you:

Opening offer: JDBs typically accept 20-40% of claimed balance.

Pre-suit: Settlement range 30-50%; avoid the suit entirely.

Post-suit, pre-judgment: 40-60%; courthouse settlement common.

Post-judgment: 50-70%; execution risk drives urgency.

Always insist on: (1) written settlement agreement identifying the specific debt, (2) dismissal with prejudice if suit was filed, (3) confirmation the account will be reported as "Paid for Less than Full Balance" or "Paid/Settled" (not "Paid in Full" unless you negotiated that), and (4) no 1099-C unless the forgiveness exceeds $600 and you accept the tax hit.

See settlement strategy playbook.

When Bankruptcy Defeats North Dakota Debt Buyers

Bankruptcy has several advantages over defending each JDB suit individually:

Automatic stay. All JDB lawsuits freeze instantly on filing under 11 U.S.C. Section 362.

Discharge. Most JDB-held consumer debt is unsecured and fully discharged under Section 727 (Ch 7) or 1328 (Ch 13).

Schedule F reaches all creditors. You do not need to track each JDB suit separately.

Proof of claim reversal. In bankruptcy, the JDB must produce the same chain-of-title documentation or the claim can be disallowed under 11 U.S.C. Section 502. You can object and win even without full litigation.

No post-discharge contact. Discharged debt cannot be collected; JDBs attempting to collect violate 11 U.S.C. Section 524 and face contempt sanctions.

See proof of debt in bankruptcy and North Dakota credit card bankruptcy.

Shell Companies and Affiliate Networks

Many JDB operations use layered corporate structures: LVNV Funding operates with Resurgent Capital; Midland Funding operates with Midland Credit Management; Portfolio Recovery uses multiple affiliates. This layering can complicate chain-of-title proofs and creates enforcement targets under North Dakota consumer statutes.

When responding to a North Dakota JDB suit, research the plaintiff's corporate parent and related entities. Inconsistent naming between the complaint, underlying agreement, and affidavit is grounds for dismissal in many North Dakota courts. See shell company deep-dive.

## Debt Buyer Rights in Ohio [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses
Source: https://debtbuyerrights.org/states/ohio.html

← debtbuyerrights.org home

Debt Buyer Rights in Ohio [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Ohio residents.

Debt Buyers in Ohio

Ohio regulates debt buyers primarily through general collection-agency rules rather than a dedicated junk-debt-buyer statute. Federal FDCPA and evidence-rule defenses still apply powerfully.

A "debt buyer" (also called a junk debt buyer, JDB, or debt purchaser) is a company that buys charged-off consumer debt from original creditors for pennies on the dollar - typically 3-5 cents per dollar face value - and attempts to collect the full balance. Common Ohio debt buyers include Midland Funding, LVNV Funding, Portfolio Recovery Associates, Cavalry SPV, and Jefferson Capital Systems.

Ohio Licensing Regime

Licensing: No state debt-buyer license; collection agencies regulated under ORC 1319.12 for certain activities.

Chain-of-title standard: Evidence rules; ORC case law requires documentation.

Applicable consumer statute: Ohio Consumer Sales Practices Act (ORC 1345.01).

Unlicensed collection activity in Ohio is itself an actionable violation in most cases - both as an independent state claim and as an FDCPA violation (because federal law prohibits collecting "by any means" that is illegal under state law).

FDCPA and Chain-of-Title Proof

Federal FDCPA (15 U.S.C. Section 1692g) and state law in Ohio generally require a debt buyer to produce:

The original cardholder agreement - proving the account existed and terms were agreed to.

Billing statements showing activity, charges, and last payment date.

Charge-off statement - the balance at the moment the original creditor wrote off the debt.

Assignment documentation - each transfer from original creditor through any intermediaries to the current plaintiff.

Bill of sale and purchase agreement showing the specific account is included in the sold portfolio.

Affidavits from each transferring entity's records custodian.

In contested Ohio cases, one or more of these links is frequently missing. Missing links = no enforceable debt. See proof-of-debt checklist.

Ohio Defenses to Junk Debt Suits

If a debt buyer has filed suit against you in Ohio, available defenses include:

Failure to state a claim. Complaint lacks specific allegations about the original creditor, assignment chain, or account details.

Standing. JDB cannot prove it owns your specific account; only owns a portfolio generally.

Statute of limitations. If the last legitimate activity was more than the state SOL years ago, the debt is time-barred. See Ohio credit card SOL.

Account stated rejection. Challenge whether the final balance was ever agreed to.

Usury/unlawful fees. Fees added post-charge-off may be challengeable.

Unlicensed collection. If the JDB lacks required Ohio licensing, collection itself may be void.

FDCPA counterclaim. Filing a time-barred suit or misrepresenting the debt can trigger $1,000 statutory damages plus attorney fees.

See SOL defense mechanics and when to fight.

Ohio Debt Buyer Settlement Economics

Ohio debt buyers paid 3-5 cents per dollar for your account. A settlement at 20-40% of face value is therefore extremely profitable for them - and still provides real relief to you:

Opening offer: JDBs typically accept 20-40% of claimed balance.

Pre-suit: Settlement range 30-50%; avoid the suit entirely.

Post-suit, pre-judgment: 40-60%; courthouse settlement common.

Post-judgment: 50-70%; execution risk drives urgency.

Always insist on: (1) written settlement agreement identifying the specific debt, (2) dismissal with prejudice if suit was filed, (3) confirmation the account will be reported as "Paid for Less than Full Balance" or "Paid/Settled" (not "Paid in Full" unless you negotiated that), and (4) no 1099-C unless the forgiveness exceeds $600 and you accept the tax hit.

See settlement strategy playbook.

Ohio Federal Bankruptcy Data

When defending a debt buyer is not enough - because multiple JDB suits are pending, or the original creditor assignments are stronger than expected - bankruptcy extinguishes the underlying debt. These FJC numbers show how Ohio debtors actually resolve junk debt.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 3,971 consumer bankruptcy cases from Ohio's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 73,53597.7%1.8%

Chapter 1343651.1%48.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

When Bankruptcy Defeats Ohio Debt Buyers

Bankruptcy has several advantages over defending each JDB suit individually:

Automatic stay. All JDB lawsuits freeze instantly on filing under 11 U.S.C. Section 362.

Discharge. Most JDB-held consumer debt is unsecured and fully discharged under Section 727 (Ch 7) or 1328 (Ch 13).

Schedule F reaches all creditors. You do not need to track each JDB suit separately.

Proof of claim reversal. In bankruptcy, the JDB must produce the same chain-of-title documentation or the claim can be disallowed under 11 U.S.C. Section 502. You can object and win even without full litigation.

No post-discharge contact. Discharged debt cannot be collected; JDBs attempting to collect violate 11 U.S.C. Section 524 and face contempt sanctions.

See proof of debt in bankruptcy and Ohio credit card bankruptcy.

Shell Companies and Affiliate Networks

Many JDB operations use layered corporate structures: LVNV Funding operates with Resurgent Capital; Midland Funding operates with Midland Credit Management; Portfolio Recovery uses multiple affiliates. This layering can complicate chain-of-title proofs and creates enforcement targets under Ohio consumer statutes.

When responding to a Ohio JDB suit, research the plaintiff's corporate parent and related entities. Inconsistent naming between the complaint, underlying agreement, and affidavit is grounds for dismissal in many Ohio courts. See shell company deep-dive.

This layering can complicate chain-of-title proofs and creates enforcement targets under Pennsylvania consumer statutes.

When responding to a Pennsylvania JDB suit, research the plaintiff's corporate parent and related entities. Inconsistent naming between the complaint, underlying agreement, and affidavit is grounds for dismissal in many Pennsylvania courts. See shell company deep-dive.

## Debt Buyer Rights in Rhode Island [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses
Source: https://debtbuyerrights.org/states/rhode-island.html

← debtbuyerrights.org home

Debt Buyer Rights in Rhode Island [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Rhode Island residents.

Debt Buyers in Rhode Island

Rhode Island requires debt buyers to hold a collection-agency license and follow state collection statutes. Unlicensed operators and those with broken chains of title can be defeated using FDCPA and state UDAP claims.

A "debt buyer" (also called a junk debt buyer, JDB, or debt purchaser) is a company that buys charged-off consumer debt from original creditors for pennies on the dollar - typically 3-5 cents per dollar face value - and attempts to collect the full balance. Common Rhode Island debt buyers include Midland Funding, LVNV Funding, Portfolio Recovery Associates, Cavalry SPV, and Jefferson Capital Systems.

Rhode Island Licensing Regime

Licensing: Collection agency license (R.I. Gen. Laws 19-14.9).

Chain-of-title standard: Evidence rules control.

Applicable consumer statute: Rhode Island Deceptive Trade Practices Act (R.I. Gen. Laws 6-13.1).

Unlicensed collection activity in Rhode Island is itself an actionable violation in most cases - both as an independent state claim and as an FDCPA violation (because federal law prohibits collecting "by any means" that is illegal under state law).

FDCPA and Chain-of-Title Proof

Federal FDCPA (15 U.S.C. Section 1692g) and state law in Rhode Island generally require a debt buyer to produce:

The original cardholder agreement - proving the account existed and terms were agreed to.

Billing statements showing activity, charges, and last payment date.

Charge-off statement - the balance at the moment the original creditor wrote off the debt.

Assignment documentation - each transfer from original creditor through any intermediaries to the current plaintiff.

Bill of sale and purchase agreement showing the specific account is included in the sold portfolio.

Affidavits from each transferring entity's records custodian.

In contested Rhode Island cases, one or more of these links is frequently missing. Missing links = no enforceable debt. See proof-of-debt checklist.

Rhode Island Defenses to Junk Debt Suits

If a debt buyer has filed suit against you in Rhode Island, available defenses include:

Failure to state a claim. Complaint lacks specific allegations about the original creditor, assignment chain, or account details.

Standing. JDB cannot prove it owns your specific account; only owns a portfolio generally.

Statute of limitations. If the last legitimate activity was more than the state SOL years ago, the debt is time-barred. See Rhode Island credit card SOL.

Account stated rejection. Challenge whether the final balance was ever agreed to.

Usury/unlawful fees. Fees added post-charge-off may be challengeable.

Unlicensed collection. If the JDB lacks required Rhode Island licensing, collection itself may be void.

FDCPA counterclaim. Filing a time-barred suit or misrepresenting the debt can trigger $1,000 statutory damages plus attorney fees.

See SOL defense mechanics and when to fight.

Rhode Island Debt Buyer Settlement Economics

Rhode Island debt buyers paid 3-5 cents per dollar for your account. A settlement at 20-40% of face value is therefore extremely profitable for them - and still provides real relief to you:

Opening offer: JDBs typically accept 20-40% of claimed balance.

Pre-suit: Settlement range 30-50%; avoid the suit entirely.

Post-suit, pre-judgment: 40-60%; courthouse settlement common.

Post-judgment: 50-70%; execution risk drives urgency.

Always insist on: (1) written settlement agreement identifying the specific debt, (2) dismissal with prejudice if suit was filed, (3) confirmation the account will be reported as "Paid for Less than Full Balance" or "Paid/Settled" (not "Paid in Full" unless you negotiated that), and (4) no 1099-C unless the forgiveness exceeds $600 and you accept the tax hit.

See settlement strategy playbook.

When Bankruptcy Defeats Rhode Island Debt Buyers

Bankruptcy has several advantages over defending each JDB suit individually:

Automatic stay. All JDB lawsuits freeze instantly on filing under 11 U.S.C. Section 362.

Discharge. Most JDB-held consumer debt is unsecured and fully discharged under Section 727 (Ch 7) or 1328 (Ch 13).

Schedule F reaches all creditors. You do not need to track each JDB suit separately.

Proof of claim reversal. In bankruptcy, the JDB must produce the same chain-of-title documentation or the claim can be disallowed under 11 U.S.C. Section 502. You can object and win even without full litigation.

No post-discharge contact. Discharged debt cannot be collected; JDBs attempting to collect violate 11 U.S.C. Section 524 and face contempt sanctions.

See proof of debt in bankruptcy and Rhode Island credit card bankruptcy.

Shell Companies and Affiliate Networks

Many JDB operations use layered corporate structures: LVNV Funding operates with Resurgent Capital; Midland Funding operates with Midland Credit Management; Portfolio Recovery uses multiple affiliates. This layering can complicate chain-of-title proofs and creates enforcement targets under Rhode Island consumer statutes.

When responding to a Rhode Island JDB suit, research the plaintiff's corporate parent and related entities. Inconsistent naming between the complaint, underlying agreement, and affidavit is grounds for dismissal in many Rhode Island courts. See shell company deep-dive.

Pre-suit: Settlement range 30-50%; avoid the suit entirely.

Post-suit, pre-judgment: 40-60%; courthouse settlement common.

Post-judgment: 50-70%; execution risk drives urgency.

Debt Buyer Rights in Texas [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Texas residents.

Debt Buyers in Texas

Texas has one of the stronger debt-buyer regulatory frameworks in the US. Junk debt buyers filing suit on purchased accounts face documented pleading and proof requirements that are often insurmountable when the original creditor's records are lost.

A "debt buyer" (also called a junk debt buyer, JDB, or debt purchaser) is a company that buys charged-off consumer debt from original creditors for pennies on the dollar - typically 3-5 cents per dollar face value - and attempts to collect the full balance. Common Texas debt buyers include Midland Funding, LVNV Funding, Portfolio Recovery Associates, Cavalry SPV, and Jefferson Capital Systems.

Licensing: Texas Finance Code Chapter 392 (debt collection) + Debt Collection Surety Bond requirement.

Chain-of-title standard: Evidence rules; Texas case law requires documentation for bills-and-notes actions.

Applicable consumer statute: Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act (Tex. Bus. & Comm. Code 17.46).

Unlicensed collection activity in Texas is itself an actionable violation in most cases - both as an independent state claim and as an FDCPA violation (because federal law prohibits collecting "by any means" that is illegal under state law).

Affidavits from each transferring entity's records custodian.

Schedule F reaches all creditors. You do not need to track each JDB suit separately.

Proof of claim reversal. In bankruptcy, the JDB must produce the same chain-of-title documentation or the claim can be disallowed under 11 U.S.C. Section 502. You can object and win even without full litigation.

No post-discharge contact. Discharged debt cannot be collected; JDBs attempting to collect violate 11 U.S.C. Section 524 and face contempt sanctions.

See proof of debt in bankruptcy and Texas credit card bankruptcy.

Shell Companies and Affiliate Networks

Many JDB operations use layered corporate structures: LVNV Funding operates with Resurgent Capital; Midland Funding operates with Midland Credit Management; Portfolio Recovery uses multiple affiliates. This layering can complicate chain-of-title proofs and creates enforcement targets under Texas consumer statutes.

When responding to a Texas JDB suit, research the plaintiff's corporate parent and related entities. Inconsistent naming between the complaint, underlying agreement, and affidavit is grounds for dismissal in many Texas courts. See shell company deep-dive.

## Debt Buyer Rights in Utah [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses
Source: https://debtbuyerrights.org/states/utah.html

← debtbuyerrights.org home

Debt Buyer Rights in Utah [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Utah residents.

Debt Buyers in Utah

Utah has one of the stronger debt-buyer regulatory frameworks in the US. Junk debt buyers filing suit on purchased accounts face documented pleading and proof requirements that are often insurmountable when the original creditor's records are lost.

A "debt buyer" (also called a junk debt buyer, JDB, or debt purchaser) is a company that buys charged-off consumer debt from original creditors for pennies on the dollar - typically 3-5 cents per dollar face value - and attempts to collect the full balance. Common Utah debt buyers include Midland Funding, LVNV Funding, Portfolio Recovery Associates, Cavalry SPV, and Jefferson Capital Systems.

Utah Licensing Regime

Licensing: Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act + Collection Agency Act.

Chain-of-title standard: Evidence rules; UT case law requires specific documentation.

Applicable consumer statute: Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act (UCA 13-11).

Unlicensed collection activity in Utah is itself an actionable violation in most cases - both as an independent state claim and as an FDCPA violation (because federal law prohibits collecting "by any means" that is illegal under state law).

FDCPA and Chain-of-Title Proof

Federal FDCPA (15 U.S.C. Section 1692g) and state law in Utah generally require a debt buyer to produce:

The original cardholder agreement - proving the account existed and terms were agreed to.

Billing statements showing activity, charges, and last payment date.

Charge-off statement - the balance at the moment the original creditor wrote off the debt.

Assignment documentation - each transfer from original creditor through any intermediaries to the current plaintiff.

Bill of sale and purchase agreement showing the specific account is included in the sold portfolio.

Affidavits from each transferring entity's records custodian.

In contested Utah cases, one or more of these links is frequently missing. Missing links = no enforceable debt. See proof-of-debt checklist.

Utah Defenses to Junk Debt Suits

If a debt buyer has filed suit against you in Utah, available defenses include:

Failure to state a claim. Complaint lacks specific allegations about the original creditor, assignment chain, or account details.

Standing. JDB cannot prove it owns your specific account; only owns a portfolio generally.

Statute of limitations. If the last legitimate activity was more than the state SOL years ago, the debt is time-barred. See Utah credit card SOL.

Account stated rejection. Challenge whether the final balance was ever agreed to.

Usury/unlawful fees. Fees added post-charge-off may be challengeable.

Unlicensed collection. If the JDB lacks required Utah licensing, collection itself may be void.

FDCPA counterclaim. Filing a time-barred suit or misrepresenting the debt can trigger $1,000 statutory damages plus attorney fees.

See SOL defense mechanics and when to fight.

Utah Debt Buyer Settlement Economics

Utah debt buyers paid 3-5 cents per dollar for your account. A settlement at 20-40% of face value is therefore extremely profitable for them - and still provides real relief to you:

Opening offer: JDBs typically accept 20-40% of claimed balance.

Pre-suit: Settlement range 30-50%; avoid the suit entirely.

Post-suit, pre-judgment: 40-60%; courthouse settlement common.

Post-judgment: 50-70%; execution risk drives urgency.

Always insist on: (1) written settlement agreement identifying the specific debt, (2) dismissal with prejudice if suit was filed, (3) confirmation the account will be reported as "Paid for Less than Full Balance" or "Paid/Settled" (not "Paid in Full" unless you negotiated that), and (4) no 1099-C unless the forgiveness exceeds $600 and you accept the tax hit.

See settlement strategy playbook.

When Bankruptcy Defeats Utah Debt Buyers

Bankruptcy has several advantages over defending each JDB suit individually:

Automatic stay. All JDB lawsuits freeze instantly on filing under 11 U.S.C. Section 362.

Discharge. Most JDB-held consumer debt is unsecured and fully discharged under Section 727 (Ch 7) or 1328 (Ch 13).

Schedule F reaches all creditors. You do not need to track each JDB suit separately.

Proof of claim reversal. In bankruptcy, the JDB must produce the same chain-of-title documentation or the claim can be disallowed under 11 U.S.C. Section 502. You can object and win even without full litigation.

No post-discharge contact. Discharged debt cannot be collected; JDBs attempting to collect violate 11 U.S.C. Section 524 and face contempt sanctions.

See proof of debt in bankruptcy and Utah credit card bankruptcy.

Shell Companies and Affiliate Networks

Many JDB operations use layered corporate structures: LVNV Funding operates with Resurgent Capital; Midland Funding operates with Midland Credit Management; Portfolio Recovery uses multiple affiliates. This layering can complicate chain-of-title proofs and creates enforcement targets under Utah consumer statutes.

When responding to a Utah JDB suit, research the plaintiff's corporate parent and related entities. Inconsistent naming between the complaint, underlying agreement, and affidavit is grounds for dismissal in many Utah courts. See shell company deep-dive.

This layering can complicate chain-of-title proofs and creates enforcement targets under West Virginia consumer statutes.

When responding to a West Virginia JDB suit, research the plaintiff's corporate parent and related entities. Inconsistent naming between the complaint, underlying agreement, and affidavit is grounds for dismissal in many West Virginia courts. See shell company deep-dive.

## Debt Buyer Rights in Wisconsin [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses
Source: https://debtbuyerrights.org/states/wisconsin.html

← debtbuyerrights.org home

Debt Buyer Rights in Wisconsin [2026]: Licensing, Chain of Title, and Defenses

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Wisconsin residents.

Debt Buyers in Wisconsin

Wisconsin requires debt buyers to hold a collection-agency license and follow state collection statutes. Unlicensed operators and those with broken chains of title can be defeated using FDCPA and state UDAP claims.

A "debt buyer" (also called a junk debt buyer, JDB, or debt purchaser) is a company that buys charged-off consumer debt from original creditors for pennies on the dollar - typically 3-5 cents per dollar face value - and attempts to collect the full balance. Common Wisconsin debt buyers include Midland Funding, LVNV Funding, Portfolio Recovery Associates, Cavalry SPV, and Jefferson Capital Systems.

Wisconsin Licensing Regime

Licensing: Collection agency license (Wis. Stat. 218.04).

Chain-of-title standard: Evidence rules control.

Applicable consumer statute: WI Consumer Act (Wis. Stat. Chapters 421-427).

Unlicensed collection activity in Wisconsin is itself an actionable violation in most cases - both as an independent state claim and as an FDCPA violation (because federal law prohibits collecting "by any means" that is illegal under state law).

FDCPA and Chain-of-Title Proof

Federal FDCPA (15 U.S.C. Section 1692g) and state law in Wisconsin generally require a debt buyer to produce:

The original cardholder agreement - proving the account existed and terms were agreed to.

Billing statements showing activity, charges, and last payment date.

Charge-off statement - the balance at the moment the original creditor wrote off the debt.

Assignment documentation - each transfer from original creditor through any intermediaries to the current plaintiff.

Bill of sale and purchase agreement showing the specific account is included in the sold portfolio.

Affidavits from each transferring entity's records custodian.

In contested Wisconsin cases, one or more of these links is frequently missing. Missing links = no enforceable debt. See proof-of-debt checklist.

Wisconsin Defenses to Junk Debt Suits

If a debt buyer has filed suit against you in Wisconsin, available defenses include:

Failure to state a claim. Complaint lacks specific allegations about the original creditor, assignment chain, or account details.

Standing. JDB cannot prove it owns your specific account; only owns a portfolio generally.

Statute of limitations. If the last legitimate activity was more than the state SOL years ago, the debt is time-barred. See Wisconsin credit card SOL.

Account stated rejection. Challenge whether the final balance was ever agreed to.

Usury/unlawful fees. Fees added post-charge-off may be challengeable.

Unlicensed collection. If the JDB lacks required Wisconsin licensing, collection itself may be void.

FDCPA counterclaim. Filing a time-barred suit or misrepresenting the debt can trigger $1,000 statutory damages plus attorney fees.

See SOL defense mechanics and when to fight.

Wisconsin Debt Buyer Settlement Economics

Wisconsin debt buyers paid 3-5 cents per dollar for your account. A settlement at 20-40% of face value is therefore extremely profitable for them - and still provides real relief to you:

Opening offer: JDBs typically accept 20-40% of claimed balance.

Pre-suit: Settlement range 30-50%; avoid the suit entirely.

Post-suit, pre-judgment: 40-60%; courthouse settlement common.

Post-judgment: 50-70%; execution risk drives urgency.

Always insist on: (1) written settlement agreement identifying the specific debt, (2) dismissal with prejudice if suit was filed, (3) confirmation the account will be reported as "Paid for Less than Full Balance" or "Paid/Settled" (not "Paid in Full" unless you negotiated that), and (4) no 1099-C unless the forgiveness exceeds $600 and you accept the tax hit.

See settlement strategy playbook.

Wisconsin Federal Bankruptcy Data

When defending a debt buyer is not enough - because multiple JDB suits are pending, or the original creditor assignments are stronger than expected - bankruptcy extinguishes the underlying debt. These FJC numbers show how Wisconsin debtors actually resolve junk debt.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,541 consumer bankruptcy cases from Wisconsin's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 795399.4%0.4%

Chapter 1358848.1%51.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

When Bankruptcy Defeats Wisconsin Debt Buyers

Bankruptcy has several advantages over defending each JDB suit individually:

Automatic stay. All JDB lawsuits freeze instantly on filing under 11 U.S.C. Section 362.

Discharge. Most JDB-held consumer debt is unsecured and fully discharged under Section 727 (Ch 7) or 1328 (Ch 13).

Schedule F reaches all creditors. You do not need to track each JDB suit separately.

Proof of claim reversal. In bankruptcy, the JDB must produce the same chain-of-title documentation or the claim can be disallowed under 11 U.S.C. Section 502. You can object and win even without full litigation.

No post-discharge contact. Discharged debt cannot be collected; JDBs attempting to collect violate 11 U.S.C. Section 524 and face contempt sanctions.

See proof of debt in bankruptcy and Wisconsin credit card bankruptcy.

Shell Companies and Affiliate Networks

Many JDB operations use layered corporate structures: LVNV Funding operates with Resurgent Capital; Midland Funding operates with Midland Credit Management; Portfolio Recovery uses multiple affiliates. This layering can complicate chain-of-title proofs and creates enforcement targets under Wisconsin consumer statutes.

When responding to a Wisconsin JDB suit, research the plaintiff's corporate parent and related entities. Inconsistent naming between the complaint, underlying agreement, and affidavit is grounds for dismissal in many Wisconsin courts. See shell company deep-dive.
